hints: Focus on what T-helper cells normally do after an antigen is presented to them, who do they help to activate?
Remember that B-lymphocytes need T-helper stimulation to divide into plasma cells and memory cells, and only plasma cells secrete antibodies.
walkthrough:
**Recall the job of T-helper cells**

Think of T-helper cells as the coordinators of the immune response. They do not make antibodies themselves, but they release cytokines to activate other cells.

Key idea: No T-helper cells = no proper activation signal.

**Link T-helpers to B-cell division**

When a B-lymphocyte meets its specific antigen, it still needs help from a T-helper cell to divide by mitosis. This division produces two important types of B-cell: plasma cells for immediate attack and memory cells for future protection.

Rule: T-helper activation -> B-cell cloning -> plasma cells + memory B-cells

**Link plasma cells to antibodies**

Plasma cells are the antibody factories. If fewer plasma cells are made, then fewer antibodies are secreted into the blood and tissue fluid.

So loss of T-helpers knocks out 1 (memory cells), 2 (plasma cells) and therefore 3 (antibodies). That gives 1, 2 and 3.

options.A: Correct. Without T-helper cells, B-cells cannot be fully activated, so both plasma cells and memory cells fall, and with fewer plasma cells, antibody production also falls.
options.B: Incomplete. It correctly includes memory and plasma cells but wrongly leaves out antibodies, which must also fall because they are made by plasma cells.
options.C: Incomplete. It correctly includes memory cells and antibodies but wrongly leaves out plasma cells, which are the direct link between T-helper help and antibody secretion.
options.D: Incomplete. It correctly includes plasma cells and antibodies but wrongly leaves out memory cells, which also depend on T-helper stimulated B-cell division.
